title: What a Hormuz Endgame Could Actually Look Like
gist: Keith Johnson argues that with renewed U.S.-Iran war parked in favor of naval and land blockades, the key endgame issue is Hormuz's navigational regime; maritime law scholar James Kraska proposes a 'Hormuz Declaration' co-led by Iran and Oman and backed by China, the U.S. and Europe, but expects a 'mowing the grass' muddle-through that keeps oil above $90.

themes.theme: Current state of Hormuz and oil

insights.claim: Trump appears to have parked the military option against Iran, relying on Operation Economic Outcast (naval blockade) and Iron Gate (land blockade of Iranian trade), per Marco Rubio.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Lower near-term escalation risk; pressure campaign continues to choke Iranian exports.
insights.locator: U.S. President Donald Trump, despite earlier threats

insights.claim: Before the February war, the Strait of Hormuz carried 20% of world seaborne oil exports; it was closed for much of this year and reopened at great cost by the U.S. Navy and shippers.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Chokepoint risk is the core driver of oil risk premium.
insights.quote: the Strait of Hormuz saw the transit of 20 percent of all seaborne oil exports in the world
insights.locator: Before the war, which began in February

insights.claim: Oil flows out of Hormuz and the broader Middle East are back to prewar averages, and with dovish Washington talk oil has fallen from $114 a barrel to the low $90s in recent weeks.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Oil has repriced ~20% lower; further downside requires a navigational settlement.
insights.quote: the global price of oil has plummeted in recent weeks from $114 a barrel to the low $90s
insights.locator: Before the war, which began in February

insights.claim: Shipping rates have fallen from autumn peaks but remain multiples of prewar levels, and Iran keeps striking tankers—two incidents in the last 24 hours.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Elevated tanker rates and war-risk insurance persist; positive for tanker owners, negative for importers.
insights.quote: they remain multiples of their prewar prices
insights.locator: But that does not portend a return to normal.

themes.theme: Hormuz as a wasting Iranian asset

insights.claim: Hormuz is Iran's greatest strategic asset but a wasting one, as Saudi Arabia and the UAE have expanded overland bypass pipelines that reduce reliance on the seaborne route.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Bypass pipeline capacity structurally lowers Hormuz leverage over time.
insights.quote: The strait is an asset of declining value for Iran

insights.claim: The July U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding punted on the strait's future navigational regime, which any negotiated end to the nine-month conflict must confront.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Navigational regime is the unresolved crux for a durable settlement.

insights.claim: Kraska's proposed Hormuz Declaration would give Iran some role but not sole control, with Iran and Oman at the forefront and major user powers—China, the U.S. and Europe—backing it, drawing on regimes like the Strait of Malacca.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: A multilateral strait regime would be the path to normal shipping costs.
insights.locator: The thrust of the argument for his

insights.claim: Kraska argues Iran's planned tollbooth on tankers, potentially worth billions annually, is a bad idea; unfreezing assets and reentering the global economy would be far more valuable for an economy with roughly 140% inflation.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Watch for frozen-asset release as a deal sweetener rather than Hormuz tolls.
insights.quote: an economy facing a dearth of imports and inflation of around 140 percent a year
insights.locator: Iran’s plan for a tollbooth in the strait

insights.claim: A negotiated international Hormuz regime would lower costs for all oil exporters and return Iran's collapsed oil exports to global markets.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: A deal is bearish oil: lower transit costs plus restored Iranian barrels.

insights.claim: Iran insists on summer conditions Trump signed off on—end of the naval blockade, end of U.S. regional military presence, end of fighting in theaters like Lebanon—while the U.S. refuses Iran any veto over Hormuz; this standoff keeps oil above $90.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Oil's $90 floor is tied to this diplomatic deadlock.
insights.quote: That standoff explains why oil remains above $90 a barrel despite an end to major combat operations in the region.

insights.claim: Kraska doubts sustained economic pressure will buckle Iran's leadership, after nearly half a century of resisting sanctions.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Don't bet on near-term regime capitulation.

insights.claim: Kraska expects a 'war-not-war' muddle-through for the next year or two with no final resolution, keeping markets on edge and prices relatively high.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Base case: persistent risk premium in oil and shipping through 2027-28.
insights.quote: I just think we will continue to muddle through over the next year or two and never get a final resolution.
